data.title: It’s Time to Bet Against Extreme Market Fear
data.description:
The key to navigating times like these in the stock market is to avoid getting caught up in the emotion, and to bet against it if you can.

The cleanest way to do that is to short the heightened fear by betting against the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), the so-called fear gauge. It has spiked in the past several days.

You can short fear by purchasing the -1x Short VIX Futures ETF (SVIX), currently trading in the 16 range. In past market crises, I have made money buying the SVIX at around 16-17, for moves back up to 24-25 as investor fears calm down.

Sentiment has darkened sufficiently to warrant getting long, or longer, both stocks and the SVIX. As always, I am using sentiment in the contrarian sense. Go long when the crowd is extremely bearish, and vice versa.

[text_ad]

Sentiment Darkens

* The Investors Intelligence Bull Bear ratio on November 17 came in at 1.83. The way I read this indicator, anything below 2 is a clear buy signal. It indicates a sentiment extreme that will revert to the mean at some point. The ratio is clearly lower now, and it will be when it reads out again soon.

* The American Association of Individual Investors sentiment indicator has printed a bull-bear spread greater than ten percentage points for four weeks in a row. For example, last week bears were at 42.2% and bulls were at 24.4% for an 18-percentage-point spread, which is greater than ten percentage points. The prior three weeks printed 20- to 30-percentage-point spreads. Check on this indicator. Sufficiently bearish to warrant getting long stocks.

* The equity put/call ratio has been printing above 1. Investors and traders buy puts (which go up when stocks decline) when they are bearish. They avoid calls (which go up when stocks advance). This ratio of puts to calls (above 1) indicates sufficient bearishness to warrant buying stocks. Previous spikes above 1 happened close to near-term lows.

* Valuations on defensive stocks are at extreme highs, while valuations on tech stocks are near extreme lows. This indicates a bearish defensive posture among investors and traders, sufficiently negative to warrant increasing long exposure.

* Much of the public (and virtually all the major podcasters, of course, because they thrive on conspiracy theories) went into irrational conspiracy theory mode surrounding the string of recent outages at various websites and in the air traffic control communications system. I doubt there was any link among them. In my experience, technology fails all the time. I am surprised people are surprised by this. A lot of it is far from perfect.

In any case, if this was part of an orchestrated attack by North Korea, Iran, Russia, or some other bad actors, the good news is they gave it a good shot, and they failed. The jump in anxiety (people reportedly stocking up on food and buying generators) contributed to the negative market sentiment mix.

Meanwhile, insiders have been getting more bullish. Buy/sell ratios for stocks on various exchanges have been continually increasing into bullish territory as the markets weaken.

2 Stocks to Watch as Fear Spikes Higher

Besides shorting fear by purchasing the SVIX, I suggest adding to any names that insiders are buying, like the stocks I suggest in Cabot Insider Edge.

Though there is no insider buying, I also think Nvidia (NVDA) looks attractive here, though I am unable to “call a bottom” in the stock. However, purchasing NVDA here gives you exposure to 75% revenue growth (just upped from 70%) for just nine times forward earnings.

In tech, I also like Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX) in the current weakness, as a bet on its AI data center capacity rental business, robotics, satellite communications and satellite launches. There is no insider buying here. But at the recent Baron Capital investor conference here in New York City, Elon Musk predicted the SPCX market cap will eventually reach the same dollar amount as global GDP. Global GDP is around $126 trillion, and the SPCX market cap is $1.75 trillion. That is quite a gap.

Of course, Musk’s forecast may well be wrong. But even if he is only partly right, it suggests solid SPCX gains over the next five or ten years. In the 115 range, SPCX is a busted IPO (it trades below the IPO price of 135). That’s the time to buy IPOs, when they are busted. Not during the initial hype.

Please note, none of this is an attempt to “call the bottom” on stocks overall or individual names referenced here. Negative sentiment can always get more negative. In extreme sell-offs, the Investors Intelligence Bull Bear ratio falls down into the 0.7 range, and it just printed at 1.83.

However, I do believe sentiment has turned negative enough to warrant getting more long exposure here, for a sentiment reversion to the mean. Most of the market is already in a correction (down 10% or more).

We’d need a recession to send it into bear market territory (down 20% or more). A recession is always possible; however, sharper minds than mine (Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research) continue to rule out a recession in the near term. For more insights on the markets and stocks that insiders like, consider subscribing to Cabot Insider Edge.

data.title: Black Friday Came Early for Stocks
data.description:
Black Friday came early for Wall Street this year.

Last week, the S&P 500 plunged 8.6%, its worst weekly performance in more than 18 months. The Nasdaq lost 10%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 8%, and the Russell 2000 small-cap index dropped 7.5%.

By Friday’s close, the S&P 500 was down more than 11% from its October high, officially putting the index in correction territory.

And the damage wasn’t limited to high-flying technology stocks.

All 11 S&P 500 sectors finished the week in the red, as you can see in the table below.

TickerSectorChange (%): Nov. 13-20
XLPConsumer Staples -2.05
XLUUtilities -3.07
XLREReal Estate -4.3
XLVHealth Care -6.15
XLYConsumer Discretionary -6.27
XLEEnergy -6.85
XLFFinancials -7
XLIIndustrials -7.35
XLBMaterials -7.45
XLCCommunication Services -7.97
XLKInformation Technology -12.49

Technology stocks were hit hardest, falling 12.5%. But industrials lost 7.4%, financial stocks fell 7%, and energy stocks dropped 6.9%. Even the traditionally defensive healthcare sector declined more than 6%.

That’s a lot of merchandise on the clearance rack.

[text_ad]

Of course, the bounce-back early this week initially reversed a lot of the selling, but the next two days gave most of that back, so there are still a lot of potential bargains in the market.

As of Tuesday’s close (and after the huge rally), 200 stocks in the S&P 500 remain in bear market territory, more than 20% below their highs.

The Best Bargains May Be Outside Technology

The current correction is being driven in large part by concerns about artificial intelligence.

And while the rebound in tech shares temporarily alleviated some of those concerns, the return of a single CEO doesn’t reverse structural concerns about circular financing or massive CapEx bills coming due in the next few years.

But given the widespread selling last week, it’s worth remembering that a broad market correction gives investors an opportunity to buy quality companies at prices that were unavailable just a few weeks ago.

History offers plenty of examples.

In March 2020, the S&P 500 plunged roughly 34% as the COVID-19 pandemic brought much of the global economy to a standstill.

Yet the market bottomed on March 23 and recovered all its losses by August.

In 2022, the S&P 500 fell roughly 25% as inflation surged and the Federal Reserve aggressively raised interest rates.
But the market eventually recovered, rewarding investors who purchased high-quality companies near the lows.

There’s no guarantee the current correction will follow the same path. But market declines have historically created some of the best opportunities for patient investors.

How to Approach the Pre-Black Friday Sale

If you’re investing with a time horizon of five or 10 years, the recent selloff should be getting your attention.

That’s not to say you should buy every discounted neocloud hand over fist just because they’re trading at a discount.

Some companies are facing legitimate business challenges. And as I cautioned on the Cabot Street Check podcast a few weeks ago, big moves should be treated as counter-trend rallies until proven otherwise.

The fact of the matter is, the S&P 500 remains below its 200-day moving average, a sign that the primary trend has weakened considerably.

Until we see the market string together a period of higher lows and higher highs, that primary downtrend should be treated as the dominant trend in the market.

But a dominant trend is not a permanent feature. After all, the long-term bias of the market remains up.

For investors looking out a few years, buying incrementally can make more sense than trying to pick a bottom.

You could establish an initial position at today’s discounted prices and reserve additional cash in case the market falls further.

Or you could build a watch list of high-quality companies and wait for signs that selling pressure is exhausted.

Either approach beats chasing stocks simply because they’re cheaper than they were a month ago.

After all, there’s no prize for being the first buyer at the bottom; sometimes it pays to wait for more confirmation of a reversal.

One More Black Friday Bargain

Of course, identifying genuine bargains takes research. And when hundreds of stocks are falling at once, separating long-term winners from potential value traps can be challenging.

That’s what we do every day at Cabot Wealth Network.

Our analysts search for opportunities across a wide range of strategies, from growth stocks and promising small caps to dividend payers and more conservative investments.

And with the market correcting or possibly even bottoming out, there could be plenty of opportunities to put those strategies to work.

For a limited time, we’re offering 40% off every Cabot investment advisory service.

Whether you’re looking to take advantage of the recent selloff, diversify your portfolio or position yourself for 2027, there’s a Cabot advisory designed to help.

Explore Cabot’s Black Friday Sale – Save 40% on All Investment Advisories

The discounts on Wall Street could get even bigger before this correction runs its course.

But for long-term investors, that’s not necessarily bad news.

data.title: 6 Thanksgiving Stocks Putting Dinner on the Table in 2026
data.description:
Thanksgiving dinner is getting more expensive again.

According to the American Farm Bureau Federation’s annual survey, the average cost of feeding 10 people a traditional Thanksgiving dinner is $58.63 this year, up more than 6% from 2025.

That’s the first annual increase since 2022, although the total remains 8.5% below that year’s record high of $64.05.

The biggest culprit is the centerpiece of the meal, a 16-pound turkey, which now costs an average of $23.68, up 10% from last year.

Milk, dinner rolls and cranberries have gotten more expensive, too.

Of course, those rising prices are bad news for shoppers. But they’re not necessarily good news for the companies selling the food.

Higher transportation, labor and commodity costs are squeezing margins throughout the food industry, and consumers are increasingly looking for bargains.

So, with Thanksgiving just a few days away, I thought it would be interesting to take a look at the companies putting dinner on the table.

[text_ad]

For our house, that means stuffing, cranberries, green beans, mashed potatoes, sweet potatoes and, of course, a nice oven-roasted (or sometimes smoked) turkey.

And since we’re more interested in stocks than recipes, we’ll break down six Thanksgiving stocks based on where they fit on the dinner table rather than where they might fit in your portfolio.

Thanksgiving Stocks on the Table This Year

Stuffing: Kraft Heinz (KHC) and Tyson Foods (TSN)

We’ll start with Kraft Heinz (KHC), the company behind Stove Top stuffing.

Stove Top has been a Thanksgiving staple for decades, providing a convenient alternative for anyone who doesn’t feel like spending hours in the kitchen preparing stuffing from scratch.

But while the brand remains a familiar fixture on grocery store shelves, Kraft Heinz has been struggling.

In the third quarter of 2026, the company reported a 2% decline in net sales and a 1.1% decline in organic sales. Adjusted operating income fell 15.2%.

That’s hardly the performance investors want to see from a company whose biggest selling point is the strength of its brands.

Last year, Kraft Heinz announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies, separating its faster-growing sauces and condiments business from its slower-growing grocery brands.

But the separation has since taken a back seat to management’s efforts to revive the underlying business. The company is now focused on restoring growth rather than committing to the previously announced split.

Consumers may love Stove Top stuffing, but that loyalty isn’t worth much to shareholders if the company can’t translate it into sales and earnings growth.

Next up is Tyson Foods (TSN), which warrants inclusion on this list due to its Jimmy Dean sausage brand.

Whether sausage belongs in stuffing is a debate that can probably wait until after dinner (Editor’s note: It absolutely does).

Tyson, meanwhile, has problems that go well beyond stuffing.

The company recently reported fiscal 2026 sales of $56.4 billion, an increase of 3.6% from the prior year. But adjusted operating income fell 14% to $1.98 billion, while adjusted earnings per share declined 17%.

The company’s chicken business has been performing well, but the beef division has been a major drag on earnings.

A historic shortage of U.S. cattle has driven up livestock costs, making it increasingly difficult for processors like Tyson to turn a profit.

The company has responded by cutting costs and reducing capacity, but there’s only so much management can do when the underlying economics of the business are working against it.

Tyson is a good example of why higher food prices don’t necessarily mean higher profits for food producers.

Mashed Potatoes: Post Holdings (POST)

Next on the menu are mashed potatoes, courtesy of Post Holdings’ (POST) Bob Evans brand.

These refrigerated mashed potatoes have become a Thanksgiving staple in our house. They’re substantially better than the instant variety and a whole lot easier than peeling, boiling and mashing potatoes yourself.

Post Holdings is also one of the more interesting businesses on our list.

The company owns a collection of food businesses spanning breakfast cereals, refrigerated products, foodservice and pet food.

Unlike some of the other companies here, Post has built much of its business through acquisitions, portfolio management and a willingness to buy or sell brands when the economics make sense.

For fiscal 2026, Post reported $8.12 billion in sales and adjusted EBITDA of $1.57 billion.

Sales were down slightly from the prior year, but the company’s refrigerated retail business is showing encouraging signs.

In its latest quarter, refrigerated side-dish volumes increased 4.7%, even as the company worked through the effects of divestitures and shifting demand elsewhere in the business.

That’s encouraging for a company selling premium convenience products to consumers who have become increasingly sensitive to grocery prices.

Management expects adjusted EBITDA of $1.45 billion to $1.50 billion in fiscal 2027, below the recently reported year’s total.

Post has shown that it can build value through acquisitions and operational improvements, but investors should keep an eye on whether those efforts translate into consistent earnings growth.

Green Beans: Seneca Foods (SENEA)

No Thanksgiving dinner is complete without something green on the table, even if it’s swimming in cream of mushroom soup and topped with fried onions.

And that brings us to Green Giant.

In years past, we could have gone one of two directions with this pick: B&G Foods (BGS), which owned the frozen Green Giant business, or Seneca Foods (SENEA), which owned the canned business.

That’s changed.

In March 2026, Seneca acquired the U.S. frozen Green Giant business from B&G for approximately $61.5 million.

That deal followed Seneca’s acquisition of the U.S. canned Green Giant business in November 2023, effectively reuniting the familiar brand’s American vegetable operations under one publicly traded company.

And that leaves Seneca as the only choice for our green beans entry.

The company is expanding its position in packaged vegetables, and it’s generating mixed results thus far.

In its latest quarterly report, the company reported sales of $897.8 million for the first six months of fiscal 2027, up from $757.5 million a year earlier.

That’s an increase of 18.5%.

Not all of that growth was organic, of course. The Green Giant acquisition contributed to the increase, and management acknowledged some supply chain and pricing challenges as it integrates the frozen business.

Gross margins also slipped from 13.7% to 12.2%.

Still, Seneca has become a more substantial player in the frozen vegetable business, and the addition of Green Giant gives it a recognizable consumer brand to complement its existing operations.

Cranberries: Ocean Spray

Love them or hate them, cranberries are a Thanksgiving fixture.

And the name most Americans associate with cranberries is Ocean Spray.

The company sells everything from fresh cranberries to canned cranberry sauce, dried cranberries and juice.

But there’s a catch for investors.

Ocean Spray is a farmer-owned cooperative, meaning you can’t buy shares.

So, while the company is an important part of Thanksgiving dinner, it won’t be part of our Thanksgiving stock portfolio.

The Turkey: Seaboard Corporation (SEB)

Now for the main event.

Butterball is one of the best-known turkey brands in America, and investors can get indirect exposure to the business through Seaboard Corporation (SEB).

Seaboard owns a 52.5% economic interest in Butterball, although it shares control of the business with its partner.

The company is also involved in pork production, commodity trading, milling and marine transportation, so Butterball is just one piece of a much larger business.

Through the first nine months of the year, Butterball benefited from higher sales prices and increased volumes.

According to Seaboard’s latest quarterly filing, Butterball’s selling prices increased 9% during the first nine months of 2026, while volumes climbed 5%.

Higher feed and transportation costs offset some of the gains, and a legal settlement weighed on third-quarter earnings. But Butterball’s operating performance has been stronger than the rising price of Thanksgiving dinner might suggest.

That makes Seaboard an interesting way to invest in the turkey business.

The problem is the stock itself.

Seaboard shares are expensive on a per-share basis and trade in relatively low volumes, which can produce sharp price swings and make it difficult for investors to establish or exit positions.

And with so many other businesses under the Seaboard umbrella, buying the stock is hardly a pure play on Thanksgiving turkey.

Dessert: Nestlé (NSRGY)

We’ll finish the meal with pumpkin pie.

And for that, we’ve got Nestlé (NSRGY), the company behind Libby’s canned pumpkin.

Libby’s has long dominated the canned pumpkin business, making it one of the most recognizable brands in the Thanksgiving baking aisle.

But buying Nestlé stock for its canned pumpkin business would be a little like buying Walmart because you enjoy its selection of Christmas decorations.

Nestlé is a global food and beverage giant, with major businesses in coffee, pet care, nutrition, confectionery and bottled water.

Libby’s is a very small part of that operation.

The company has also been working through a challenging period of slower consumer spending, cost pressures and restructuring.

But its latest results suggest that some of those efforts are beginning to pay off.

Nestlé reported organic sales growth of 3.7% through the first nine months of 2026, including 4% growth in the third quarter.

More encouragingly, real internal growth, which measures sales growth excluding price increases, accelerated to 2.8% in the latest quarter.

Nestlé’s improving volume trends suggest consumers are responding to its brands, although management still has work to do restoring margins and improving the performance of slower-growing businesses.

The company expects full-year organic sales growth of 3% to 4% and free cash flow above 9 billion Swiss francs.

For long-term investors looking for exposure to a diversified collection of global consumer brands, Nestlé deserves a closer look.

Just don’t expect canned pumpkin sales to move the needle.

Which Thanksgiving Stocks Are Worth Buying?

If I were shopping for stocks based on this year’s Thanksgiving dinner, I’d spend the most time looking at Post Holdings (POST), Seneca Foods (SENEA) and Nestlé (NSRGY).

Post has an interesting portfolio and a history of using acquisitions to build its business. Seneca has expanded its position in the packaged vegetable market, while Nestlé is showing signs of improving underlying demand.

Seaboard’s Butterball business looks attractive, but the stock’s limited liquidity makes it a tougher proposition.

And Ocean Spray, unfortunately, isn’t an option unless you’re planning to become a cranberry farmer.

As for my actual Thanksgiving shopping list, I’ll stick with the usual suspects.

I don’t mind paying a little more for the turkey. Just don’t mess with the stuffing.

[author_ad]

*This post has been updated to reflect current market conditions.

data.title: The 3 Most Volatile Stocks Today
data.description:
The stock market has taken a brutal turn in November, and volatility has come roaring back.

As of Friday’s close, the S&P 500 fell more than 11% from its early October highs, officially entering correction territory. The Nasdaq has fared even worse, dropping 18% from its peak and wiping out all its gains for 2026.

And Wall Street’s favorite fear gauge, the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX), has surged from below 20 in mid-November to nearly 36 to end the week.

Much of the selling has been concentrated in technology stocks, particularly the high-flying AI names that drove the market higher earlier this year.

And while the broader market has suffered, some of the most volatile stocks have been absolutely hammered.

That’s a good reminder that when the market turns against you, owning the wrong stocks can turn an ordinary correction into a brutal portfolio drawdown, so it’s a good time to identify which stocks are most vulnerable to those swings.

To screen for the most volatile stocks today, I looked for large-cap stocks with a beta of at least 2—meaning they’re twice as volatile as the general market. And I stuck with large-cap companies since small-cap stocks are typically more volatile and unpredictable.

[text_ad]

My screen produced a total of 42 stocks with betas above 2, 16 of which had betas north of 3 (meaning they’re three times more volatile than the S&P 500).

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the most volatile stocks on the list had betas above 4, with the top stock boasting an astronomical beta of 6.3.

So with that in mind, here are three of the most volatile stocks today, ranked from least to most volatile. Unsurprisingly, all three of them have been major beneficiaries of the AI boom.

The 3 Most Volatile Stocks Today

Volatile Stock #3: Nebius (NBIS)

Nebius has become one of the market’s most volatile ways to bet on the AI infrastructure boom.

The company operates an AI cloud platform, providing the computing power and infrastructure needed to train and run artificial intelligence models. And business has been booming.

In its third-quarter earnings report, Nebius reported revenue of $981 million, an increase of 571% from a year ago. The company also expects revenue to reach $12 billion to $13 billion in 2027, roughly four times its projected 2026 sales.

But that growth comes at an enormous cost.

Nebius expects to spend approximately $27 billion on capital expenditures this year, followed by another $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027. That’s an extraordinary amount of money for a company that generated just $530 million in revenue in 2025.

The company expects customer prepayments and financing backed by its contracts to cover most of that spending. But those projections depend on continued demand for AI infrastructure, access to financing and the company’s ability to bring new data center capacity online.

And investors have become increasingly skeptical of the massive spending commitments being made across the AI industry.

To wit, NBIS shares plunged more than 16% on November 20 alone as the broader AI selloff intensified.

With a beta of 4.93, Nebius moves nearly five times faster than the S&P 500, so investors should be prepared for a wild ride.

Volatile Stock #2: Sandisk (SNDK)

Sandisk has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI-fueled memory boom, with shares up 216% in the last year. And that’s after a 69% decline from the stock’s all-time highs in June.

In its fiscal first-quarter earnings report, Sandisk reported revenue of $11 billion, up an astonishing 378% from a year ago. Data center revenue alone surged to $4.8 billion, up 61% from the previous quarter.

But even those blowout results haven’t been enough to protect the stock from the recent AI selloff.

Shares tumbled 13.5% following the October 29 earnings report, despite the company beating expectations. And on November 20, SNDK plunged another 16% as investors reacted to warnings that NAND flash memory prices could fall in 2027.

That’s a particularly troubling development for Sandisk, whose extraordinary earnings growth has been driven in large part by soaring memory prices.

With a beta of 6, investors should expect plenty more volatility, regardless of whether the AI bull market resumes in earnest.

Volatile Stock #1: CoreWeave (CRWV)

CoreWeave is the final entry on our list of volatile AI buildout names, and its beta of 6.3 puts it at the top, making it six times more volatile than the S&P 500.

CoreWeave is one of the neocloud companies that sits directly in the AI infrastructure buildout, renting high-performance GPU capacity to companies that need massive compute power. The concern is that expectations are extremely high, and any perceived threat to future AI infrastructure demand can punish the stock quickly, as we’ve seen over the last few months.

As of the close on Friday, shares had fallen more than 70% from their all-time high and were actually trading below their IPO price of $40 per share.

Of course, Monday morning’s massive snap-back rally has reversed some of those losses, with shares up 20% on the day as I write this.

Bottom Line on the Most Volatile Stocks Today

With momentum-driven stocks, there’s no telling when enthusiasm may dry up and leave investors hungry to capture profits. And as we’ve seen recently, that profit-taking can quickly turn into a rush for the exits if the tune of the market changes.

It’s entirely possible that tech stocks have gotten oversold, and that Friday’s brutal selloff will turn out to be the final flush before the market resumes its push higher.

But if you’re a longer-term investor looking for stability, these volatile stocks are probably best avoided.

[author_ad]

data.title: What’s Wrong with Gold?
data.description:
Soaring bond yields and plunging AI stocks have dominated the headlines lately, in turn causing another pertinent trend to be somewhat ignored: falling precious metal prices.

Given investors’ persistent worries over inflation and geopolitical activity, it might seem paradoxical that gold prices are weakening, instead of strengthening, in this environment. After all, it’s an established maxim that gold is a typically reliable safe haven for investors seeking inflation protection.

But there’s always an exception to every rule of thumb in the investing markets, and we’re seeing one play out right now in the metals and mining space.

[text_ad]

Gold’s problem, as I see it, is threefold: The first one involves its currency component as reflected in the U.S. Dollar Index (USD). The dollar’s surprising show of strength on the international currency market in the face of domestic inflation has perplexed many participants—not least gold investors. But rising U.S. retail prices aside, a strengthening USD is usually a fairly serious headwind for gold to battle, which is proving to be true now.

It’s also important to remember that inflation doesn’t always necessarily weaken the dollar on the international currency front. Currency valuations are influenced by relative interest rates, monetary policy expectations, economic growth, capital flows and the relative performance of other major economies. This means the dollar can strengthen even when inflation remains elevated in the everyday U.S. economy, particularly if inflation in other countries is worse or U.S. interest rates are expected to remain relatively high.

The key point here is that a strengthening DXY (The USD as measured against a basket of currencies) makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies. That relationship is particularly relevant in the current environment.

This brings us to the second of gold’s current problems; viz., investor sentiment. While it may seem counterintuitive, investor positioning in the gold market remains surprisingly—and stubbornly—bullish despite its recent price declines.

Indeed, this has been a thorn in the side of the gold market for some time this year. My go-to measure for retail investor sentiment on physical gold is the JM Bullion Fear and Greed Index, which remained firmly in “greed” territory as of November 19, with a 66% bullish reading. This is significant since it registers the opinions of actual physical gold coin and bullion bar customers.

By contrast, the latest Kitco Weekly Gold Survey (published November 13) shows a significant deterioration in bullish sentiment from a week earlier, when 68% of respondents expected gold prices to rise. The latest survey found that just 42% expressed optimism on gold; however, the bulls still outpaced the bears (38%), with 21% of respondents neutral.

Elsewhere, a report from the World Gold Council found that global physically backed gold ETFs attracted another $2.7 billion in October, with European gold ETFs attracting $1.8 billion and Asian ETFs bringing in $1.3 billion. However, North American funds experienced marginal outflows while global gold bar-and-coin demand declined 19% year over year in Q3, suggesting that longer-term institutional and strategic demand remains relatively resilient, while individual physical-gold buyers have become more hesitant (potentially long-term bullish from a contrarian perspective).

But what I think provides a more telling overview of the near-term gold sentiment backdrop is FX research platform WatchTower Terminal’s November 16 retail positioning report. The latest data showed that a whopping 84% of retail traders are currently long gold versus just 16% short. From a contrarian standpoint, this heavily one-sided retail positioning is disturbing—at least for the short-term outlook.

All told, I believe we’ll need to see significant deterioration in the near-term bullish positioning for gold futures and physical gold before a meaningful near-term bottom can be established. Clearly, we’re not there yet, so additional gold price weakness is still possible.

Finally, gold is likely being hindered by the need for investors to raise cash in the face of falling worldwide equity prices. What we’re now seeing can probably best be described as a classic liquidation market where participants are scrambling to raise cash as the AI trade unwinds and economic growth concerns intensify. This, in turn, means even defensive-minded investors may be forced to liquidate at least some of their gold holdings in order to cover losses or margin calls in other assets.

In other words, gold’s traditional safe-haven appeal can temporarily take a back seat to investors’ more immediate need for cash.

We’ve seen this scenario play out many times in past bearish market environments—including during the 2008 credit crash, which saw gold prices plunge along with virtually everything else. But what often happens in such cases is that once selling pressures are finally exhausted and markets return to a semblance of normalcy, gold is among the first of the major asset classes to launch a recovery rally.

This especially holds true when inflation and geopolitical worries remain persistent, as is the case today. And the reason behind the historical tendency for gold to launch a strong post-crash recovery is that investors eventually remember that gold remains undisputed as a haven against inflationary pressures and geopolitical fears. What’s more, if gold continues to weaken as the global market sell-off intensifies, it will undoubtedly be recognized as a major bargain once the dust finally settles.

In conclusion, my answer to the question, “What’s wrong with gold?” is “Nothing at all.” It’s my contention that gold’s loss of safety appeal with investors is merely temporary. Moreover, I look for the yellow metal’s safe-haven appeal to return en force once the current equity market turbulence subsides.

data.title: Best Stocks Under $10 to Buy Now
data.description:
Before I get into the best stocks under $10 to buy right now, let me start with this disclaimer: share price doesn’t really matter.

As Warren Buffett is fond of saying, “Price is what you pay, value is what you get.” That’s true. Still, for someone starting a portfolio with just a couple thousand dollars, investing in 50 shares of a $10 stock seems way more appealing than investing in one share of a $1,000 stock.

If you want to diversify, you don’t want to devote half your portfolio to one share of Amazon (AMZN) or Alphabet (GOOG). You can create a portfolio of 10 stocks even if you only have $2,000 or $3,000 to invest.

To do it, however, you need to find low-priced stocks.

[text_ad]

From there, it depends on what you’re looking for in your investments: long-term gains or a quick return in a prime turnaround stock candidate.

If you want to find the best stocks under $10 that you can buy and hold for a while, you should start with stocks that have already been trending upward for some time. A strong chart, after all, is one of the best indicators of future gains. For that, I screened for stocks with share prices under $10 that are trading above their 50-day moving average. There were quite a few on the list, which was a bit of a surprise given the weak market of late, so I narrowed it down to companies with a potentially powerful “story” (as my colleague Mike Cintolo would call it) as well.

Best Stocks Under $10: Algonquin Power & Utilities Corp. (AQN)

Algonquin is a Canadian utility company that provides everything from electricity to water to wastewater collection, plus natural gas utility systems and transmission. It serves 1.27 million customers in not only Canada but the U.S., Chile and Bermuda. It has operations in 14 U.S. states. The company is on track for 7.6% revenue growth and 5.9% EPS growth this year with earnings growth accelerating to 13.9% next year (with 4.2% revenue growth). Meanwhile, the stock (a mid-cap) trades at just 14x forward earnings and less than 1x book value, despite a 10% rally since the start of September. Shares trade for just 5.50, and the average one-year price target among analysts is 6.32 – a 15% premium to the current price. A 4.7% dividend yield adds to AQN’s appeal.

Best Stocks Under $10: Coty Inc. (COTY)

Coty sells well-known beauty products in the U.S. and overseas. The company has two divisions: Prestige and Consumer Beauty. Its products include fragrances, cosmetics, skin and body care, etc., manufacturing, marketing and selling brands such as Burberry, Calvin Klein, Hugo Boss, Marc Jacobs, Tiffany and many others. Department stores, drug store and e-retailers are among its more prominent clients.

And while Coty’s sales have slipped in recent years, it has become far more profitable, with earnings on track to expand from 21 cents a share last year to 36 cents a share this year. The stock has risen accordingly, up 40% year to date and more than doubling from less than 2 per share in June to exactly 4 per share now. Of course, COTY used to be a $13 stock as recently as 2024, so it’s really just getting up off the mat. The lack of top-line growth is concerning, but the stock is cheap at just 11x forward earnings and 0.6x sales. Coming off a good quarter (61% earnings growth) and with plenty of momentum in the share price, it’s worth a low-priced flyer.

Best Stocks Under $10: Peloton Interactive (PTON)

Remember during Covid when this company (along with Zoom, Chegg and a few other online-only outfits) was all the rage? That didn’t last, even though plenty of folks (myself included) still own and use Pelotons, the interactive subscription exercise bikes and treadmills. But sales are down 40% from those Covid peaks, declining from a high of $4 billion in 2021 to $2.44 billion in the recently completed 2026 fiscal year. And the stock has been eviscerated, plummeting from a high above 150 a share in late 2020 to just 5 a share now. It seems the selling may have been overdone – the company is profitable for the first time in years, and those profits are expected to more than double in FY ’27 (to 38 cents a share from 14 cents on an adjusted basis last year). A $600 million debt refinancing plan earlier this month gave shares an extra boost – and the company a jolt of much-needed cash. Also, sales actually increased 2% in the latest (fiscal first) quarter – a third consecutive quarter of sales growth, an encouraging sign. Plus, free cash flow more than doubled.

Trading at less than 14x forward earnings and 1x sales, PTON looks like a strong buy-low candidate … with a very low share price.

data.title: Don’t Miss the Opportunity in Fixed-Rate Investments
data.description:
This market is increasingly volatile and troubling.

The S&P 500 is now down more than 6% from the high and could be headed to correction territory (down 10%). Several issues are shaking things up.

The already struggling technology trade is getting slapped with a controversy at Nvidia (NVDA). At the same time, tensions with Iran are increasing and investors still can’t decide if the Democratic takeover of Congress is good or bad for the market.

But perhaps the most troubling aspect of the current market is interest rates. The benchmark 10-year Treasury rate soared above 5% in September and October to the highest level since 2002. While the rate has since come off the high, it still hovers above 5%, the level at which the market considers problematic.

The Treasury rate is the benchmark used for mortgages, car loans, personal loans, and any kind of longer-term interest rate. Higher loan rates make borrowing less affordable and increase costs for businesses. That’s a big part of the reason 84% of stocks on the S&P 500 fell 10% or more from the high and 60% of stocks fell at least 20% after the Treasury rate moved above 5% earlier this fall.

Interest rates had trended lower for forty years prior to this decade. The benchmark 10-year Treasury rate went from an astronomical 16% in 1981 all the way down to about 0.5% in 2020 during the pandemic. The downward trend was unmistakable, although bouncy at times.

That downward trend ended in 2022. The rate went from 1.5% at the beginning of the year to 4.23% by October. The rate had averaged between 2% and 2.5% over the decade prior. What happened? Inflation happened.

Inflation puts upward pressure on interest rates as fixed-rate investors demand to be compensated. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), by which inflation is usually measured, averaged 1.77% from 2000 through 2019. The inflation rate skyrocketed to over 9% by June of 2022, the highest level in more than 40 years. But inflation has since moderated.

The CPI inflation rate fell to less than 4% by the middle of 2023 and averaged under 3% from late 2024 until early this year. CPI has moved higher and averaged around 3.5% since March because of the inflationary pressures of high oil prices as a result of the war with Iran.

While inflation has come down, interest rates have not. The 10-year Treasury rate had peaked at just about 5% in October of 2023, after which it started trending lower. But the rate has now eclipsed the previous peak.

It is for good reason that rates have moved higher while inflation has come way down since 2022. Virtually no one expected the astronomical inflation rates to last, and they haven’t. Bond rates don’t get priced to compensate investors for 10 years of an inflation rate that is likely to come way down in a matter of months.

But here we are four years later, and the inflation rate is still double the average of what it was in the first two decades of this century. The long-lingering higher inflation does require compensation to fixed-rate investors.

[text_ad]

The high energy prices have lingered for more than eight months now. The increased inflationary pressure prompts the Fed to get aggressive and counter those pressures by raising the fed funds rate. Higher short-term rates also put upward pressure on longer rates.

There are also demand pressures. Higher demand tends to increase prices, and interest rates are the price of money. Technology companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to fund data centers and other AI infrastructure. That creates competition for fixed rates while the government continues to sell massive amounts of bonds to fund its ungodly amount of debt.

It’s also a strong economy. Third-quarter GDP was 3.4%, the highest growth in years and well above the average growth rate of the past decade. Forecasts for fourth-quarter GDP are also quite bullish. A stronger economy puts upward pressure on interest rates, and demand for borrowing increases.

Of course, the war with Iran will end at some point. That should drive oil prices, and likely interest rates, lower. But for now, interest rates are still near the highest level in two decades. Therein lies the opportunity. The same situation that spells trouble for borrowers also presents opportunity for income investors.

Prudent investors don’t put all their investable assets in stocks, especially older ones in a lower risk class. Earning a good return on your non-stock invested assets will bolster your overall returns and make it easier to stay invested in turbulent stock markets. Plus, these assets can also provide a much-needed income. But it’s been so long since decent returns on safe assets were available that many investors have forgotten about this important aspect of portfolio management.

Fixed-income yields are now near the highest level since the beginning of this century. Quality fixed-income investments are no longer paying a measly 2%. Now, you can get investment-grade-rated bonds and preferred stocks paying 5%, 6% or even 7%. And they have less downside now, with rates near a multi-decade high.

It’s true that interest rates can still move higher from here, and prices of fixed-income securities will fall if they do. But higher interest rates from here will likely put pressure on the market and the economy. That pressure would likely drive interest rates lower. Also consider that fixed-income investments generally have a longer holding period than most stocks. Even if interest rates trend higher in the near term, they are far less likely to average higher than they are today over the next five years or so.

The recent interest rate spike is presenting a golden opportunity to lock in the highest rates in decades and partially fill the fixed-income void for most investors.

[author_ad]

data.title: 3 High-Dividend Stocks with Impressive Growth
data.description:
When investors think about growth stocks, they usually picture fast-growing technology companies that reinvest their profits to expand their businesses.

Contrast that with dividend stocks, the slow-moving investments that provide steady income but relatively little appreciation.

But as we’ve seen this year, that’s not always the case.
High-dividend stocks, as measured by the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF (VYM), have significantly outperformed growth stocks this year. VYM’s one-year return of 16.5% is more than double the 7.6% return of the Nasdaq and more than four times greater than the 3.1% return of the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS).

And when you combine those rising stock prices with years of dividends, the returns can be surprisingly strong.

That’s particularly attractive for investors looking to generate income without giving up the opportunity for capital appreciation.

Consider three stocks from very different industries: Altria Group (MO), Aegon (AEG) and NLI Holdings (NL).

All three currently offer dividend yields above 5%. And all three have produced positive returns over the past year and the past five years.

Let’s take a closer look.

[text_ad]

3 High-Dividend Stocks Boasting Solid Total Returns

1. Altria Group (MO): Big Dividends and Big Returns

Altria is one of the best-known dividend stocks on the market.

The company owns Marlboro, one of the most recognizable cigarette brands in the United States, along with several other tobacco and nicotine products.

Cigarettes aren’t exactly a growth industry. Smoking rates have been declining for decades, and tobacco companies face ongoing regulatory pressure.

But Altria has managed to generate substantial cash flow despite those challenges, largely because of its pricing power and established brands.

And much of that cash goes directly to shareholders.

Altria recently raised its quarterly dividend by 4.7%, to $1.11 per share, or $4.44 annually.

At a recent share price just shy of 79, that works out to a dividend yield of 5.6%.

Even more impressive, Altria has increased its dividend 61 times over the past 57 years.

But investors haven’t just been collecting dividends.

Over the past year, Altria has delivered a total return of 45.3%, including reinvested dividends.

And over the past five years, its total return is 156% (with dividends reinvested).

That’s an exceptional performance for a company operating in an industry with declining demand.

Of course, any investment thesis has to factor in the biggest drag on shares: Cigarette sales volumes continue to decline, and the company’s success thus far has relied on the expansion of its smoke-free products.

Still, Altria’s combination of dependable cash generation, a long dividend history and strong stock performance makes it worth a look for income investors.

2. Aegon (AEG): An Insurance Stock with Strong Long-Term Growth

Aegon is a major Dutch international financial services company (although shareholders approved a plan to redomicile to the U.S. some time next year) with operations in life insurance, retirement products and investment management. Its businesses include Transamerica, a well-known provider of insurance and retirement services in the United States.

The company has been working to simplify its operations, improve profitability and return more money to shareholders.

And those efforts are producing results.

In the first half of 2026, Aegon’s operating earnings rose 9% to €804 million, while operating capital generation increased 27%.

The company also reported a 54% increase in new individual life insurance sales at Transamerica.

Those improvements are helping support a growing dividend.

Aegon raised its interim dividend for 2026 by 11%, to €0.21 per share. Based on its last share price just shy of 8.50, the stock offers a trailing dividend yield of about 5.7%.

And the shares have been strong as well. Over the past year, Aegon has generated a 15.3% total return, including reinvested dividends.

Five-year returns are even stronger, totaling 124% with dividends reinvested.

That’s an impressive longer-term return for a company in a relatively mature industry.

Of course, it’s worth noting that insurance companies are sensitive to changes in interest rates and the performance of their portfolio assets. A significant market downturn could put pressure on earnings.

Still, Aegon’s improving operations, growing dividend and strong five-year returns make it an interesting choice for investors seeking both income and growth.

3. NLI Holdings (NL): A Little-Known Dividend Stock

The third company on our list is probably unfamiliar to most investors.

NLI Holdings (NL), formerly known as NL Industries, is a small, diversified holding company involved in industrial products and chemicals.

Its businesses include a controlling interest in CompX International, which manufactures security products and components for the marine industry.

NLI also owns a significant stake in Kronos Worldwide, a producer of titanium dioxide, a chemical used in paints, plastics and other industrial products.

It’s not an especially glamorous business. But that doesn’t mean you should ignore it.

NLI has benefited from improving results at both CompX and Kronos.

In the third quarter of 2026, the company reported net income of $12.7 million, or $0.26 per share, compared with a loss of $7.8 million, or $0.16 per share, a year earlier.

CompX’s quarterly sales rose 10%, while its segment profit increased from $4.8 million to $6.4 million.

Meanwhile, Kronos reported an 18% increase in quarterly sales, helped by market-share gains and higher selling prices.

The company currently pays a quarterly dividend of $0.10 per share, or $0.40 annually.

With shares recently trading around 7.30, that translates to a dividend yield of 5.6%.

The dividend has increased from $0.07 per quarter in 2023 to $0.10 today. The company also made special dividend payments in 2024 and 2025, so there’s a strong shareholder-friendly bent to the company when business conditions allow.

And the stock has produced respectable returns.

Over the past year, NL has delivered a total return of 36%, including dividend reinvestment.

Over the past five years, its total return with dividends reinvested is 51.6%. So while it hasn’t been quite as strong as the other names on this list, it’s put up solid numbers just the same.

It should be noted, however, that NLI is a relatively small company, with a market capitalization of roughly $350 million. As a result, shares are very thinly traded and require special handling and more time to get into and out of positions.

The company’s earnings also depend heavily on industrial demand and the performance of its subsidiaries, so an economic slowdown would be a major drag on shares.

Nevertheless, NLI offers a combination of high income and improving financial results that could appeal to investors willing to consider smaller stocks.

High Dividends Don’t Have to Mean Low Growth

One of the biggest misconceptions about dividend investing is that investors must choose between income and growth.

But investors who focus only on fast-growing companies that pay little or no dividend may be overlooking some attractive opportunities.

Altria, Aegon and NLI Holdings operate in very different industries, yet all three have rewarded shareholders through a combination of dividend income and stock appreciation.

For investors seeking steady income without giving up the potential for growth, they’re three stocks worth watching.

[author_ad]

data.title: Why Value Stocks Are Beating Growth Stocks for the First Time in a Decade
data.description:
Value stocks are having a banner year.

The Vanguard Morningstar Value ETF (VTV) is up 20% year to date, putting it on track for its best year since 2021 (23.7% return). But it’s not just the performance in value stocks as an asset class that’s been impressive; it’s their outperformance of growth stocks and the broad market that truly stands out.

As of trading last Friday, November 13, the tech- and growth-heavy Nasdaq was up just 9.4% so far this year. The last time the VTV topped the Nasdaq was a decade ago, in 2016, when the 14.1% run-up in value stocks more than doubled the 5.9% return in the Nasdaq that year.

As mega-cap tech names, the Mag. 7 and now artificial intelligence plays have gained in prominence in recent years, value stocks have often been left in the dust. The performance hasn’t been bad, mind you; entering 2026, the average annual return in the VTV in the 2020s was just under 9%, roughly in line with the historic annual return in the S&P 500. But it paled in comparison to the performance in growth stocks, with the Nasdaq up 177% since the beginning of 2020.

[text_ad]

This year, that script has been flipped.

Why Investors are Pivoting to Value Stocks

The AI trade has finally run into some skepticism as investors worry that companies are spending far more than they’re earning, and the general public fears that AI might take their jobs, bring environmentally harmful data centers to their towns or even “kill us all,” as a couple industry whistleblowers warned. Meanwhile, the war in Iran has sent prices – particularly oil prices – back into the stratosphere, forcing the Fed to raise interest rates again. That has put a damper on growth. But with the economy still doing fine and the bull market very much intact, investors haven’t gone away. They’ve simply pivoted to the many undervalued and unloved names that had been left in the dust the last few years as Wall Street drooled over AI.

This year, however, investors have shifted their gaze away from AI, at least since the furious April-May run-up. And what they’ve found are a lot of growing companies in non-AI industries that are trading at relative bargains.

I compare what has happened in 2026 to when my wife and I take our kids’ iPads away for a week. At first, they complain; but then, they find other things to do – play soccer and football outside, play hide-and-seek inside, ride their bikes down to the nearby country store to get Poppis (“healthy,” prebiotic-infused soda for kids) and a cider donut. Usually, they have way more fun once they stop staring at screens and start looking at (and enjoying) everything else around them – a lesson we all (myself included!) could probably learn from in this screen-heavy era.

Value Is Beating Growth … But Another Growth Rally Would Help

It’s not a perfect comparison. After all, the AI boom has delivered some fantastic, wealth-building profits over the last few years. But for those of us who seek value and prioritize having a diverse portfolio, it has not been as fruitful as it was for those investors with nothing but AI and Mag. 7 stocks in their portfolio. Or at least it wasn’t until this year. Now, after a decade of underperformance, value investors are being rewarded. It’s why six stocks in my Cabot Value Investor newsletter portfolio have reached my price target this year, including two in the last month alone.

Hopefully there will be many more winners to come as value stocks continue to outperform. And even if the AI trade isn’t dead, and tech and chip stocks come roaring back … value stocks will probably do just fine, like they did during the aforementioned April and May rally.

Value stocks are a good place to be right now. If you need help finding the right ones, you can join me at Cabot Value Investor by clicking here.

data.title: Value Investing Opportunities in a Stealth Bear Market
data.description:
This year has witnessed one of the most paradoxical market environments in memory. Although the major indexes, led by the S&P 500, have remained buoyant through much of 2026, below the surface there has been what can only be described as a “stealth” bear market. But through the mixed performance and periodic volatility spikes, the market has also provided value-oriented investors with opportunities, which we’ll discuss here.

A Stealth Bear Market Is Hiding in the S&P 500

But first, consider that while the S&P has spent much of the last couple of months around 2-3% below its all-time high, more than 40% of S&P 500 stocks were at least 20% below their 52-week highs as of earlier this month. Even more tellingly, the average individual stock listed on the NYSE has entered bear market territory, trading roughly 21% below its 2026 peak, even though the headline indexes have masked much of this damage.

What this suggests is that we’re witnessing a classic internal correction in the broad market, with a relatively small group of mega-cap leaders keeping the SPX elevated even as most of its component stocks are underperforming. And the reason for the broader weakness isn’t hard to discover: It’s primarily related to surging longer-dated Treasury yields.

Indeed, the so-called “risk-free” discount rate for the 10-year Treasury isn’t far below the recent highs of 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. And since higher discount rates reduce the present value of future earnings and cash flows, it makes stocks appear less attractive at existing prices.

It’s no surprise, then, that the last several weeks have witnessed a soaring number of NYSE stocks making new 52-week lows, with many days showing new lows in the triple digits while new highs are sometimes merely low-double digits. Many of those new lows are bond funds or interest rate-sensitive equities.

Why AI Stocks Are Under Pressure

But while some rate-sensitive industries are still experiencing selling pressure, formerly strong AI-related names have lately been victims of the stealth bear, and for obvious reasons: Recent fears that the AI trade is “overdone” continue to percolate as of mid-November.

[text_ad]

On that score, remaining under selling pressure as of this writing is one of the market’s core proxies for the AI buildout, Nvidia (NVDA), which fell to a 16-month low on November 12 after the sudden resignation of its CEO. The stock’s recent plunge reminded everyone that the all-things-AI trade remains tenuous after what looked like a possible “wash-out” bottom of the leading AI infrastructure and support stocks earlier this month.

As for why specifically investors are in panic mode over AI stocks, conventional thinking suggests that the market is moving from rewarding AI spending and growth potential to demanding evidence that the enormous investments in AI infrastructure—to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars—will lead to worthwhile returns. Additional reasons include fears over the data center builders’ increasing reliance on debt financing—with the aforementioned rising interest rate environment contributing to these fears—as well as uncertainties over how quickly AI adoption will be monetized.

But here’s another possible reason: physical AI data center overbuilding. According to statistics from Cleanview, 68% to 75% of all tracked (mainly hyperscale) data centers in the U.S. aren’t yet operational and are either actively under construction or in the planning or announced phases. That’s a substantial development pipeline, and there’s no guarantee that all of this planned capacity will ultimately be needed or prove economically viable.

And while I may be stretching the analogy, I think it’s somewhat comparable to China’s infrastructure and property overbuilding trend of recent years that led to a prolonged property slump in that country.

Thus, it can be argued the market is worried that today’s oversized investments based on projections of future AI demand may not see the predicted returns materialize as quickly—or as strongly—as developers and investors anticipate.

To that end, a July study by McKinsey found that portions of the AI infrastructure ecosystem exhibit “bubble-like characteristics,” particularly among highly leveraged AI infrastructure intermediaries and companies with negative cash flow. And if the aforementioned debt financing and related interest rate concerns persist, this could make future financing more expensive and difficult to attain, thus amplifying the damage from increased worries over the overbuilding aspects of the data center boom.

As a result of these salient factors, I think avoiding the temptation to jump in and buy the beaten-down AI names is ideal right now. Instead, I suggest that tech sector participants wait for the semiconductor indexes and ETFs to confirm a bottom instead of assuming the worst is over for the AI sector.

Where Value Investing Opportunities Are Emerging

That said, even within the current “stealth bearish” environment, the market has provided some attractive opportunities for value-oriented investors. Indeed, many of the turnaround stocks in our Cabot Turnaround Letter portfolio have benefited in recent weeks from the recent rotation towards value stocks in the wake of the AI crash. And that’s because beaten-down value stocks are often among the biggest beneficiaries of broad market weakness, as investors gravitate toward deeply discounted, previously overlooked equities—particularly those with strengthening financial profiles—in anticipation of an eventual market rebound.

And it’s worth noting that most beneficiaries of a confirmed market bottom are typically those stocks and industry groups that did the best job of resisting the selling pressure during the correction period. And right now, many of the stocks fitting that description are in the defensive healthcare and consumer staples sectors.

To that end, these two areas are where I see the most opportunity for turnaround-focused investors going forward and where I suggest participants looking to hedge their tech sector exposure look closely.

[author_ad]
